intro: Haydn opens with a quiet exchange between winds and strings, then lets two violins slip into the quick movement before the orchestra catches up. Serge Koussevitzky conducts the Boston Symphony Orchestra in this 1929 recording.

sections.label: Intro · Winds and low strings answer
sections.mNote: Short phrases in G major prepare the quick movement

sections.label: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
sections.mNote: Vivace assai: the quiet opening bursts into G major

sections.label: Dev · The opening tune changes key
sections.mNote: Broken chords carry the violins through minor keys

sections.label: A′ · B minor opens into G major
sections.mNote: Repeated B notes become part of the home chord

cues.title: Winds speak, strings answer
cues.text: A two-bar phrase in the winds meets a two-bar answer from low strings. The strings turn towards D major; when the exchange comes round again, they return to G. Haydn marks this little conversation Adagio cantabile.
cues.evidence: Adagio cantabile, bars 1–17, described in the movement-by-movement score discussion: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Two violins steal away
cues.text: The Vivace starts quietly in the two violin sections, still leaning towards D major. Four bars into the new tempo, the whole orchestra lands on G. The bass holds that G while the notes above it grow quicker.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 18–30: violin opening, tonic arrival in bar 22 and held G in the bass. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: London, March 1792
cues.text: The new symphony reaches its first audience on 23 March 1792, during Haydn’s first London visit. Johann Peter Salomon is organising the concerts; across town, Haydn’s pupil Ignaz Pleyel is providing music for a rival series.
cues.evidence: Première date: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn). Salomon’s concerts and Pleyel’s rival engagement: Orrin Howard, LA Phil programme note, https://www.laphil.com/works/symphony-no-94-surprise

cues.title: The tune takes a detour
cues.text: The development begins with a variant of the first tune. Then loud broken chords take over, travelling from A major through D minor, B♭ major and G minor. The violins have left the exposition’s easy dance behind.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 107–140; the broken-chord passage begins at bar 123. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: B becomes part of G
cues.text: The approach to the return closes in B minor. Haydn keeps repeating B, then places G beneath it: the same note now belongs to G major. The first tune comes home almost under cover.
cues.evidence: Vivace assai, end of development and recapitulation from bar 154: B minor cadence and repeated B sounding with G. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A hush, then the Vivace
transitions.from: Intro · Winds and low strings answer
transitions.to: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
transitions.how: The introduction reaches a dominant seventh on D. The first violins lead out with falling quavers, and the metre changes from 3/4 to 6/8. Both violin sections begin the Vivace quietly; only four bars later does the full orchestra arrive forte on G, which the bass holds for nine bars.
transitions.evidence: Adagio cantabile and Vivace assai, bars 1–30, especially the dominant seventh, falling violin figure and tonic arrival in bar 22. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: The first tune starts travelling
transitions.from: A · Two violins, then the orchestra
transitions.to: Dev · The opening tune changes key
transitions.how: The exposition’s D major close dwindles to repeated B notes in the first violins. A variant of the first tune starts the development. The later broken chords begin abruptly on A major, then turn through D minor, B♭ major and G minor before a chromatic descent.
transitions.evidence: Vivace assai, end of exposition and development, bars 99–153. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

transitions.title: The first theme comes home
transitions.from: Dev · The opening tune changes key
transitions.to: A′ · B minor opens into G major
transitions.how: A descending chromatic passage reaches F♯ major, then resolves to B minor. The repeated B notes continue, but G joins them and turns them into the third of the home chord. The first tune returns in G major, with its repetitions shortened.
transitions.evidence: Vivace assai, bars 134–154 and the recapitulation: F♯ major, B minor and the concealed return to G. https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/94._Sinfonie_(Haydn)

source.title: Haydn, Symphony No. 94, full score (Leipzig: Breitkopf & Härtel, ed. Rietz, plate 8876, [1855])
source.locator: Adagio cantabile — Vivace assai, printed pp. 1–18: wind-and-string introduction, violin opening and orchestral returns.

timeline.note: Oboes and bassoons sing above a held horn note. Low strings answer; a flute joins the repeated wind phrase.
The two violin sections start the Vivace quietly on their own.
The full orchestra lands forte on G, with trumpets and timpani.
The first tune returns in G major; the full orchestra follows the violin opening.

fields.label: Work version
fields.note: The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.value: 22 and 24 April 1929: the first side on 22 April, the second side on 24 April
fields.note: Young’s discography lists the first side (CVE-48983-2) with the 22 April 1929 session and the second side (CVE-48986-2) with a later recording date of 24 April 1929 for the published retaken side. DAHR’s list for 24 April 1929 includes CVE-48986 and Bolig gives take 2 for the second side. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

fields.label: Place
fields.value: Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States
fields.note: Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.note: Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.value: Side 1: CVE-48983, take 2 (22 April 1929); side 2: CVE-48986, take 2 (24 April 1929)
fields.note: Young gives CVE-48983-2 and CVE-48986-2 as the issued takes of the first movement’s two sides. Bolig independently gives CVE-48986 take 2 for part 2. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files.
fields.note: The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Haydn died in 1809. This is a term calculation, not a worldwide clearance or a statement about an unidentified modern edition.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis).
fields.note: Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

quote.text: The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I.
quote.source: London notebook, after his benefit concert on 4 May 1795; our translation

composer.background:
On 4 May 1795, Haydn gave a benefit concert at the King’s Theatre in London. The programme included his new D major Symphony, now numbered 104. Afterwards he entered the result in his notebook: “The whole company was extremely pleased, and so was I. I made four thousand gulden this evening. Such a thing can only be done in England.” He was sixty-three, a wheelwright’s son who had spent most of his adult life wearing an Esterházy servant’s livery.

Haydn was born in Rohrau in 1732. His father made wheels, played the harp by ear and sang; his mother had worked as a cook. At about six, Joseph left home for schooling in Hainburg. By 1740 he was a choirboy at St Stephen’s Cathedral in Vienna. Singing gave him a daily education in church music, though little instruction in composition. It also gave him chances to find a meal at performances outside the cathedral. When his voice broke and he was dismissed in 1749, another musician, Johann Michael Spangler, took him into his family’s crowded room.
